title: Karah prashad
hookLine: a warm sweet of flour, butter and sugar is given to everyone into cupped hands

lines: A STEEL BOWL ALONG THE ROWS.
cards: Near the end of the service, the prayer called Ardas is said, everyone standing. Then a small stir.

Someone comes along the rows with a large steel bowl, and everyone around you holds out two hands, cupped together, like a little bowl of their own. Into your hands goes a warm, soft, glossy lump of something golden.
It smells of toasted flour and butter. It's sweet, and still warm. What is it, and why does everyone get exactly the same?

teach.h: KARAH — THE PAN. PRASHAD — A GIFT.
teach.b: It's karah prashad. Karah is the large iron pan it's cooked in. Prashad means a gift, grace, something blessed and given.

It's equal parts whole wheat flour, ghee, which is clarified butter, and sugar, with water. The flour is roasted in the ghee until golden, the sugar syrup goes in, and it's stirred until thick and shining.

The Sikh code of conduct asks that whoever makes it keep clean and recite Gurbani, the Guru's words, while it cooks. So the sweet is made with prayer in it. In the service it's placed before the Guru Granth Sahib.
After the Ardas, a Sikh touches it with a kirpan, a small sword, as a sign of acceptance, and then it's shared out. Here's the point: everyone gets it.
The Sikh in the front row, the visitor at the back, the rich donor, the person who wandered in off the street. In the Gurus' Punjab, caste rules often kept people from eating from the same dish.
Sikhs understand karah prashad, like the langar, as setting that aside on purpose.
Same bowl, same sweet, same portion, into everyone's hands.
A few practical things. You receive it with both hands cupped and eat it there, often wiping your hands on a small tissue after.

It's rich, so if you only want a little, quietly say thora, meaning a little, and the server will give you less. Declining it altogether is considered impolite, so asking for a small amount is better.

how: After Ardas, karah prashad, a sweet of equal parts flour, ghee and sugar made while reciting Gurbani, is touched with a kirpan and served to everyone present alike into cupped hands.

o: a spiced tea poured for guests at home
a festival dessert made only for Vaisakhi
a blessed sweet given alike to all, after Ardas

games.q: what's inside the sweet — tap the pairs.

s: karah prashad is given only to Sikhs
everyone present receives it, visitors included.
it's made of equal parts flour, ghee and sugar
roasted and stirred with water while Gurbani is recited.
it's fine to refuse it outright
declining is considered impolite; ask for a little, thora, instead.

games.q: the server with the steel bowl reaches you. you've just eaten and don't want much. what do you do?
o: cup your hands and ask for a little.
take a full portion and leave it on the floor.
games.why: cup both hands and say thora, a little. declining altogether is considered impolite; a small portion is fine.

practice: If you have something sweet nearby, a piece of fruit, a square of chocolate, a spoon of honey, hold it in your cupped hands; if not, just cup your empty hands in your lap and look at the bowl they make.
Think of everyone in the world receiving something today, all given the same amount as you. Then, if you have it, eat it slowly, as a gift.

wordCard.voice: Karah prashad. The warm sweet of flour, ghee and sugar, given to everyone alike, into cupped hands.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the sweet offering from the iron pan, given to all.

carryVoice: Your line: sweet, shared, equal. Two cupped hands, and no one gets more. Day one hundred forty-two, done.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, Akal Takht (preparation and distribution of karah prashad)
